Get started with alphaN in Stata

Source: vignettes/articles/stata.Rmd
stata.Rmd

alphan is the Stata version of the R package alphaN. It sets the significance level of a regression coefficient as a decreasing function of the sample size, so that a significant result corresponds to at least a chosen Bayes factor in favor of the alternative hypothesis. This page goes through every subcommand. The same steps in R are in Get started in R.

Installation 

net install alphan, from("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jespernwulff/alphaN-stata/main/")

The command is written for Stata 14 or later and has been tested on StataNow 19.5. Nothing else needs to be installed. To update an existing installation, add the replace option. After installation, help alphan opens the help file, which is also on this site.

Calibrating the significance level

We are planning a regression with 1,000 observations. By default, alphan finds the level at which rejecting the null hypothesis means the null and the alternative are at least equally likely, a Bayes factor of 1, which rules out Lindley’s paradox.

alphan 1000
Significance level calibrated to a Bayes factor       method: JAB

           n |         BF       alpha
-------------+------------------------
       1,000 |          1   .00858227

Raising the target asks for more evidence before you are allowed to reject, which lowers the level. A Bayes factor of 3 is conventionally called moderate evidence and 10 strong evidence. The bf() option takes a list.

alphan 1000, bf(1 3 10)
Significance level calibrated to a Bayes factor       method: JAB

           n |         BF       alpha
-------------+------------------------
       1,000 |          1   .00858227
       1,000 |          3   .00254915
       1,000 |         10  .000691139

Sample sizes are also a list, and the level falls as they grow.

alphan 100 1000 10000 100000, bf(3)
Significance level calibrated to a Bayes factor       method: JAB

           n |         BF       alpha
-------------+------------------------
         100 |          3   .00910357
       1,000 |          3   .00254915
      10,000 |          3  .000731456
     100,000 |          3  .000213299

The result is left in r(alpha), and the whole table in r(table), for use in the rest of a do-file.

alphan 1000, bf(3)
display r(alpha)
Significance level calibrated to a Bayes factor       method: JAB

           n |         BF       alpha
-------------+------------------------
       1,000 |          3   .00254915

.00254915

Choosing the prior

The method() option selects the prior behind the Bayes factor. jab, the default, min, robust and balanced invert Jeffreys’ approximate Bayes factor with different choices of the prior. For instance, balanced balances the Type I and Type II errors, assuming realistic effects are uniform between 0 and upper().

alphan 1000, bf(3) method(balanced)
Significance level calibrated to a Bayes factor       method: balanced
realistic effects: uniform on [0, 1]

           n |         BF       alpha
-------------+------------------------
       1,000 |          3     .024221

The methods es and moment calibrate to the effect-size and moment Bayes factors of Klauer, Meyer-Grant and Kellen (2025), whose priors center the alternative on an effect size you choose with de(). Because the moment prior assigns zero density to the null value itself and little to effects near it, the level it implies falls much faster with the sample size.

alphan 100 1000 10000, bf(3) method(es) de(.5)
alphan 100 1000 10000, bf(3) method(moment) de(.5)
Significance level calibrated to a Bayes factor       method: ES
prior: de = .5, nu = 3, r = .2887

           n |         BF       alpha
-------------+------------------------
         100 |          3    .0118502
       1,000 |          3   .00218956
      10,000 |          3  .000580671

Significance level calibrated to a Bayes factor       method: moment
prior: de = .5, nu = 5

           n |         BF       alpha
-------------+------------------------
         100 |          3   .00787684
       1,000 |          3  .000491352
      10,000 |          3  .000020322

For a regression, give p(), the number of other estimated coefficients including the intercept, to obtain the calibration that is exact for the normal linear model. Choosing a calibration discusses how to pick a method and a target.

Joint F tests of several coefficients take q(), the number of coefficients tested. The targeted effect is then on Cohen’s f scale, so de(sqrt(.15)) targets a medium effect.

alphan 200, bf(3) method(es) q(2) p(2) de(sqrt(.15))
Significance level calibrated to a Bayes factor       method: ES
prior: de = .3873, nu = 3, r = .1581, q = 2 (joint F test), p = 2

           n |         BF       alpha
-------------+------------------------
         200 |          3   .00842742

From regression output to Bayes factors

alphan jab, typed after an estimation command, reports Jeffreys’ approximate Bayes factor for every coefficient except the intercept.

sysuse auto, clear
regress price mpg weight i.foreign
alphan jab
(1978 automobile data)

      Source |       SS           df       MS      Number of obs   =        74
-------------+----------------------------------   F(3, 70)        =     23.29
       Model |   317252881         3   105750960   Prob > F        =    0.0000
    Residual |   317812515        70  4540178.78   R-squared       =    0.4996
-------------+----------------------------------   Adj R-squared   =    0.4781
       Total |   635065396        73  8699525.97   Root MSE        =    2130.8

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       price | Coefficient  Std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
         mpg |    21.8536   74.22114     0.29   0.769    -126.1758     169.883
      weight |   3.464706    .630749     5.49   0.000     2.206717    4.722695
             |
     foreign |
    Foreign  |    3673.06   683.9783     5.37   0.000     2308.909    5037.212
       _cons |  -5853.696   3376.987    -1.73   0.087    -12588.88    881.4934
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Jeffreys' approximate Bayes factor after regress      method: JAB
n = 74

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
         Coefficient |           b  Std. err.        t     P>|t| BF (H1 vs H0)
---------------------+---------------------------------------------------------
                 mpg |   21.853604  74.221139     0.29    0.7693         .1214
              weight |   3.4647058  .63074896     5.49    0.0000        414367
           1.foreign |   3673.0604  683.97827     5.37    0.0000        212603
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The last column is the Bayes factor in favor of the alternative. mpg is far from significant, and the Bayes factor of 0.12 says more: the data are about eight times as likely under the null hypothesis. Name a coefficient to report only that one, and choose another prior with method().

alphan jab weight, method(min)
Jeffreys' approximate Bayes factor after regress      method: min
n = 74

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
         Coefficient |           b  Std. err.        t     P>|t| BF (H1 vs H0)
---------------------+---------------------------------------------------------
              weight |   3.4647058  .63074896     5.49    0.0000        586004
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The command works after any estimator that stores e(b), e(V) and e(N). It uses the standard errors of the fitted model, so a vce() option carries over.

logit foreign mpg weight
alphan jab

       _cons |   13.70837   4.518709     3.03   0.002     4.851859    22.56487

If all you have is a result reported in a paper, convert the statistic or the p-value. With df(), alphan jabp reads the p-value as coming from a t test; without it, from a z test.

alphan jabt 2.695, n(200)
alphan jabp .007038863, n(200) df(190)
Jeffreys' approximate Bayes factor                    method: JAB

           n |          t          BF
-------------+------------------------
         200 |     2.6950      2.6707

Jeffreys' approximate Bayes factor                    method: JAB
p-value from a t test

           n |          p          BF
-------------+------------------------
         200 |  .00703886      2.8938

alphan klauerbf does the same for the effect-size and moment Bayes factors. Here is a t statistic of 2.24 on 79 degrees of freedom, against an alternative centered on a medium effect.

alphan klauerbf, n(80) t(2.24) de(.5)
Klauer et al. (2025) Bayes factor                     method: ES
prior: de = .5, nu = 3, r = .2887

           n |          t          BF
-------------+------------------------
          80 |     2.2400      1.5678

Power at the calibrated level

A lower level costs power. alphan power gives the power of the coefficient test at the calibrated level against a standardized effect d(), the quantity that the t statistic divided by the square root of the sample size estimates.

alphan power 1000, d(.1) bf(3)
alphan power 1000, d(.1) bf(3) method(balanced)
Power at the calibrated significance level            method: JAB

           n |          d          BF       alpha       power
-------------+------------------------------------------------
       1,000 |         .1           3   .00254915      0.5547

Power at the calibrated significance level            method: balanced

           n |          d          BF       alpha       power
-------------+------------------------------------------------
       1,000 |         .1           3     .024221      0.8172

A report for your preregistration

alphan report records every input, the resulting level, the decision rule, the power against the effects you care about and the references to cite. Add saving(report.md, replace) to write it to a file.

alphan report 1000, bf(3) method(es) de(.5) p(4) powerat(.1 .5)
# alphaN settings report

Generated on 2026-11-08 with alphaN for Stata 0.3.0.

## Inputs

- Sample size (n): 1,000
- Target Bayes factor: 3 (moderate evidence)
- Calibration method: ES: effect-size Bayes factor of Klauer,
  Meyer-Grant & Kellen (2025)
- Targeted effect size (de): 0.5 (Cohen's d)
- Prior degrees of freedom (nu): 3
- Prior scale (r): 0.2887
- Retained model parameters (p): 4 (effective sample size 996)
- Scope: exact for the normal linear model (evaluated at the effective
  sample size n - p); asymptotic for other generalized linear models.

## Result

- Calibrated alpha level: 0.0022
- Decision rule: Reject H0 if the two-sided p-value of the coefficient
  is at or below 0.0022.
- Interpretation: a significant result then corresponds to a Bayes
  factor of at least 3 in favor of the alternative under this prior.

## Power at the calibrated alpha

- Against a standardized effect of 0.1: 0.53
- Against a standardized effect of 0.5: 1.00

## Please cite

- Wulff, J. N., & Taylor, L. (2024). How and why alpha should depend on
  sample size: A Bayesian-frequentist compromise for significance
  testing. Strategic Organization, 22(3), 550-581.
  doi:10.1177/14761270231214429
- Klauer, K. C., Meyer-Grant, C. G., & Kellen, D. (2025). On Bayes
  factors for hypothesis tests. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 32,
  1070-1094. doi:10.3758/s13423-024-02612-2

Graphs

alphan plot compares the level across sample sizes. Other twoway options are passed through, and the data in memory are left alone.

alphan plot, bf(3) methods(jab min robust balanced es moment)

plot of chunk unnamed-chunk-16

alphan powerplot shows what each calibration costs in power, with every method at its own level and a fixed .05 as the dashed reference.

alphan powerplot, d(.1 .5) bf(3) methods(jab min robust balanced es moment)

plot of chunk unnamed-chunk-18

alphan jabplot shows how the Bayes factor maps onto the p-value at a given sample size. The triangle marks the level for your target; the dotted lines mark the levels for Bayes factors of 1, 3 and 10.

alphan jabplot 1000, bf(3)

plot of chunk unnamed-chunk-20
